newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Post-apartheid South Africa looks east.
newsitem.headline: Post-apartheid South Africa looks east.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela flew home on Monday after a 10-day trip to Southeast Asia aimed at touting southern Africa as a destination for Asian investment.

Mandela, heading a 115-member delegation of officials and businessmen, witnessed the signing of trade agreements in the Philippines and Malaysia, asked Brunei to sell oil to Pretoria, and discussed technical assistance, air travel, and financial guarantee pacts in Singapore.

Throughout his journey, Mandela emphasised the importance of establishing links between the fledgling South African Development Community (SADC) and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
"The Southern African Development Community...is itself seized of the question of expanding links with ASEAN," Mandela said in a speech to Malaysian businessmen at the weekend.
ASEAN -- which comprises Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- is developing a free trade area by the year 2003.
The 12-member SADC, currently chaired by South Africa, has similar ambitions.

The SADC which groups Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Malawi, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Swaziland, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe, represents 40 percent of Africa's population and 80 percent of the continent's GDP.
The two groups have a combined population of 600 million.
Malaysians are leading the charge into South Africa and are the fourth-biggest source of foreign investment, behind traditional partners Britain, the United States and Germany.
Malaysian firms have committed 6.0 billion rand ($1.35 billion) since April 1994, when South Africa's first universal-suffrage democratic elections were held.
That does not include a likely Malaysian stake in the privatisation of South Africa's Telkom telecommunications firm.

Last week, the South African government announced it was holding final negotiations with a consortium grouping U.S.-based SBC Communications and state-run Telekom Malaysia to sell a 30 percent stake in Telkom. Analysts have estimated the value of the stake at more than six billion rand ($1.35 billion).

Three Malaysian firms at the weekend signed joint-venture deals with South African firms, including one between Malaysia's ABI Construction and South Africa's Trakprops 31 for a mixed development project in Cape Town valued at $1 billion.
Malaysian businessmen say South Africa's good infrastructure and position as gateway to the African market are important.
When Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir took office 16 years ago he launched a "Look East" policy that drew a huge influx of Japanese investment.
Minerals and Energy Affairs Minister Penuell Maduna said during the tour South Africa may buy oil from Southeast Asia and welcomed investments in South African petrochemical projects.
Malaysia and Brunei are oil exporters and Singapore is the region's premier refining centre.

South Africa is Singapore's largest African trading partner, accounting for almost one-third of its trade with the continent. Bilateral trade was Singapore $945 million ($659.4 million) in 1996 with Singapore's exports comprising 65 percent of the total.
Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong led a business delegation to southern Africa this month to look at building airports, resorts, toll roads, as well as mining ventures in the region.
